judgments.rationale: The conjugate-modulus identity and the subsequent elimination/solution of the complex equations are the only mark-earning methods; trigonometric and proof tags are not independently required.
Convergence and the first acceptable term are determined with a geometric series and logarithmic threshold reasoning; no separate Calculus limits method is assessed.
The recurrence/geometric sequence and the explicitly marked induction proof are central; logarithmic rearrangements are intermediate algebra rather than a separate assessed skill.
The markscheme separately rewards the palindromic polynomial structure, quadratic factors, and complex roots; unsupported sequence, matrix, and statistics tags are excluded.
The local-minimum question earns its marks by interpreting and applying the derivative, not by an independently assessed inverse-function or graph-transformation method.
Function composition, inverse/domain conditions, completing the square, and the associated inequality are the marked methods; the algebraic skills are correctly secondary to Functions.

The plane work earns vector-product and scalar-product marks, while part (c) separately awards a compound-angle identity and sine-rule/rationalization marks; all three current skills are materially assessed.
The marked work is the series/limit argument and the definite-integral area/volume calculation; trigonometric expressions and the rotation angle are not separate skills.
Every substantive mark comes from expanding the binomial and applying it to the compound-interest expression; exponent notation and the one-step calculation are not separate tags.
All marks are awarded for setting up, evaluating, and applying a definite integral to the area between the two curves.
The question uses intersection/independence probability calculations; no distinct conditional-probability formula is required by the marked method.
The frame areas form and are summed as a geometric sequence, while the separately marked median is descriptive statistics and is therefore secondary.
The Euler-form manipulations and extraction of real parts are complex-number methods; trigonometric notation and exponent notation are supporting representation only.
Part (a) uses logarithm laws/monotonicity and part (b) is a complete induction proof of the logarithmic inequality; inverse-function work is not marked.
The substitution requires differentiating y=vx, then separating and integrating variables to solve the homogeneous differential equation.
The card counts form an arithmetic sequence and all substantive parts use its formula, sum, divisibility, and integer-row consequences; the 60-degree diagram is contextual.
The density, probabilities, quartiles, mode/median, and linear expectation/variance are statistical; repeated marked integration is an independently assessed Calculus secondary.
Inverse construction/domain is primary; the separately marked finite-series limit and final area integral are retained as Number-and-algebra and Calculus secondaries.
The marked task is identifying the period and graph behavior of a transformed tangent function; no inverse-function or independent trigonometric-identity method is required.
Regression-line/mean-point work is descriptive statistics and the final standardization is a normal-distribution method; the sequence tag is unsupported.
The tangent gradient is obtained by differentiation and the angle condition applies that derivative to locate the possible points; the supplied radian angle is contextual.
Graph/domain/intercept and inverse evaluation are function methods; cotangent/secant rewriting and the trigonometric solve earn a genuine Geometry-and-trigonometry secondary.
The assessed methods are position/velocity vectors and their magnitudes followed by a triangle-based descent-angle calculation; no Calculus method is marked.
Every part uses Euler-form complex numbers, modulus/argument, and complex representation; the resulting sine form is not an independent trigonometric topic.
The question repeatedly constructs probability-generating polynomials for discrete variables; ball-selection counting and polynomial representation are distinct supporting methods.
The investigation is curvature via first/second derivatives, extrema, limiting behavior, and implicit differentiation; quadratic expressions are examples, not a separate quadratic-solving method.
Inverse functions, graph transformations, and composition dominate; marked logarithmic/algebraic manipulation and the final area integral are correctly secondary.
The roots, modulus/argument, and Argand work are all complex-number methods; no independent triangle/trigonometry method is marked.
The sine-rule/double-angle work is used within a triangle-geometry problem; triangle geometry is the defining assessed method.
The markscheme explicitly uses conditional probability and independence/probability-model calculations.
The question is a quadratic-equation task; the candidate’s topic correction is accepted with Quadratics under its controlled Number-and-algebra owner.
After establishing the distance expression, the sole substantive task is optimizing it by differentiation.
Divisibility by a repeated linear factor is handled through a double-root/remainder condition for a polynomial; no independent quadratic solve is required.
The marked work is reading the arccos graph and its equation/domain behavior; the contextual triangle/trigonometry tags are not independently assessed.
The contradiction is established by forming a quadratic inequality and proving its square is nonnegative on the interval; proof, quadratic, and inequality methods are all marked.
Both parts are regression-line calculation and prediction, which are descriptive statistics; statistical inference is not used.
Normal-distribution work dominates, while the box and box-count parts independently use binomial discrete probability models.
Density/normalization/median are continuous-RV work; integration by parts and the l’Hopital limit are Calculus secondaries, and the equal-team count is combinatorial.

Implicit differentiation, domain/tangency analysis, and the 4-mark solid-of-revolution volume are all marked; the recommendation omitted the independently assessed integration/application-of-integration method.
The distances and angle are solved with triangle geometry/Pythagorean and cosine-rule relationships; vector and coordinate tags are not independently required.
Decreasing intervals and concavity are obtained from first and second derivatives, both direct applications of differentiation.
Depreciation/compound-interest powers and logarithms are marked, and the threshold is found from an inequality; no sequence/series method is assessed.
Maximum speed and the second-direction-change acceleration use derivative applications, but part (b) explicitly awards marks for the definite integral giving total distance.
The complete marked method relates segment, triangle, and sector areas and uses the angle in radians; coordinate geometry is not used.
The question’s substantive work is the sequence behavior and its term/sum relations; graph presentation is contextual.
The distribution table is used to compute and interpret mean/variance-style descriptive quantities; no sequence method is independently assessed.
The planes are intersected using vector normals and line/plane relationships; matrix-system elimination is not treated as an independent tag here.
The later section solves a homogeneous differential equation by partial fractions/integration, while the earlier curve analysis separately marks differentiation and graph features.
The flat/spherical comparison uses vector products, spherical-triangle angles, and arc length measured in radians.
The convergence/term relations are sequence-and-series work; limits, descriptive statistics, and quadratics are not independently marked.
The parallelogram/plane construction is solved entirely with vector equations and products.
The complex roots/geometry are handled through complex-number methods; the trigonometric form is representational.
The supplied graph is used to establish inverse restrictions and evaluate the inverse; graph reading is supporting context rather than a separate tag.
The double-angle identity and interval solve are primary trigonometry; the resulting quadratic in cos(theta) is a materially assessed Number-and-algebra secondary.
Tangency is determined from the zero-discriminant condition of the resulting quadratic, exactly matching the markscheme.
All three parts are normal-distribution standardization/symmetry questions; Probability models is not independently assessed.
The question asks for graph transformations such as reflection/reciprocal effects; no inverse-function method is independently marked.
The solid-of-revolution volume is an application of integration and the integral setup/evaluation itself is separately marked; the rotation angle is not a radian-measure skill.
The complete solution is in complex numbers; trigonometric notation is only the representation used in the complex method.
The central task is the limit, while the markscheme independently allows a fundamental trigonometric limit/identity method; it is a secondary, not a Calculus skill.
The cosine/sine-rule relationships are the complete marked method within triangle geometry.
Velocity/acceleration applications, the limiting velocity, and the separately marked definite-integral race distances are all assessed; the recommendation omitted the core Integration tag.

The binomial model is explicitly recognized and repeatedly used, conditional probability is explicitly marked, and the weighted independence calculation is a probability model; the recommendation wrongly drops the discrete-RV method.
The markscheme separately marks integration by parts, a first-order differential equation, derivative-based curve sketching, and tangent gradients.
Factor/remainder-theorem work is the complete method; inverse-function context is not independently assessed.

The distribution and expected value are discrete probability-model work, mode/mean are descriptive statistics, and identifying the first-50-customer convenience sample assesses sampling/inference terminology.
